I'm a 72-year-old farmer in Quzhou County with a high education level and 55 years of experience. Let me think through my season.

At my age, I've seen good years and bad years, droughts and floods, price booms and collapses. My 10.1 mu farm has been in my hands for over half a century. I know every corner of it — which patch holds water, which dries out first. My three-person household means my wife and I do most of the work, though we hire a few days of labor during harvest and transplanting when timing is critical.

My cropping system:
- **5 mu of winter wheat → summer maize double cropping** (the standard Quzhou system, gives me grain security)
- **5.1 mu of chili peppers** (my cash crop, better returns than cotton if prices hold, but risky)

**Wheat (5 mu):**
I plant wheat in mid-October after preparing the land. Last year I got about 480 kg/mu, and the soil still looks decent. I'm targeting around 500 kg/mu this year if spring rain cooperates. I'll apply compound fertilizer as base — about 18 kg N/mu equivalent split between base and topdress. At jointing, if the wheat looks yellow, I'll add another 8-10 kg urea per mu. Irrigation: I'll irrigate at wintering, jointing, and grain-filling — three times total. The well water costs money but three irrigations is my standard; less and I risk the yield. Seed: I'll use the improved Jinmai variety I've been using for three years, saved seed mostly, but I refresh with about 30% purchased seed to avoid degeneration. Seed cost is low, about 15 yuan/mu.

**Maize (5 mu, same land after wheat harvest):**
The turnaround after wheat harvest in early June is brutal — usually 5-7 days. I hire a custom combine for wheat harvest (saves me days), then immediately till lightly and plant maize. I plant a hybrid yellow corn variety, not the fancy GMOs (not available here anyway), just the reliable local hybrid that's done well. I broadcast about 15 kg N/mu as base fertilizer at planting, then one topdress at the 8-leaf stage if it doesn't rain. Maize is less work than wheat but needs that one critical irrigation at tasseling/silking. I'll irrigate twice if it's dry — once at seedling stage and once at tasseling. Yield target: 450 kg/mu, which is conservative but realistic on this land after wheat.

**Chili (5.1 mu):**
Chili is where I make my money, but it's also where I gamble. I start seedlings in a small nursery in late March (I have a simple plastic tunnel I built years ago). I transplant in late April to early May, after the last frost risk. This takes a lot of labor — my wife and I do most of it, but I hire 3-4 days of help for transplanting because timing is everything; if you're late, prices crash by harvest.

For chili, I apply more fertilizer than grain crops — about 20 kg N/mu, 8 kg P/mu, 10 kg K/mu. I split it: base fertilizer (compost + compound fertilizer) at transplanting, then two topdresses during fruiting. I use drip irrigation on the chili plot — I invested in cheap drip tape five years ago and it paid for itself in water savings and yield. I'll irrigate 8-10 times through the season, especially during flowering and fruit set.

Pesticides: chili gets fungicide twice (anthracnose is the killer here) and insecticide as needed (aphids, borers). I scout my fields every morning — at my age, the walk is good for me anyway. I also apply herbicide once before transplanting.

Chili harvest is multiple picks from July through September, sometimes into October. I dry them on the concrete yard in front of my house. Yield expectation: 300 kg/mu of dried chili if the weather holds.

**Budget and tradeoffs:**
I'm spending about 2,800 yuan on fertilizer across all crops, 900 yuan on hired labor, 600 yuan on pesticides, and 500 yuan on seeds. The drip irrigation on chili saves water but the pumping still costs about 400 yuan for the season. Total input cost around 5,500 yuan. It's a lot for a 10-mu farm, but at my age, I know that under-investing costs more than over-investing. Still, I'm not buying any new equipment this year — my old tools work fine, and I need cash in reserve for medical expenses. My wife and I are getting older; a hospital bill could wipe out a year's profit.

The big risk is chili prices. If they crash, I'm in trouble. But I've been growing chili for 20 years; I know the buyers, and the local chili market is stable. Wheat and maize are my insurance — they won't make me rich, but they'll feed my family.
